1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SQS: Simple Queue Service; SNS: Simple Notification Service; EFS: Elastic File System; AZ: Availability Zone; TCP: Transmission Control Protocol; UDP: User Datagram Protocol; TLS: Transport Layer Security; WAF: Web Application Firewall; ACM: AWS Certificate Manager; CDN: content delivery network; DAX: DynamoDB Accelerator; TTL: time to live; RDS: Relational Database Service; FIFO: first in, first out; SMS: Short Message Service; JMS: Java Message Service; AMQP: Advanced Message Queuing Protocol; MQTT: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport; STOMP: Simple Text Oriented Messaging Protocol; ECS: Elastic Container Service; EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service; ECR: Elastic Container Registry; REST: representational state transfer; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; IAM: Identity and Access Management; SAM: Serverless Application Model; SFTP: Secure File Transfer Protocol; FTPS: File Transfer Protocol Secure; FTP: File Transfer Protocol. Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) is the AWS name for the family of load balancers in this note: the Application, Network and Gateway Load Balancers.

  • Design event-driven, microservice and multi-tier architectures
  • Choose scaling strategies: horizontal or vertical, stateless or stateful
  • Pick the services for loose coupling: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, MQ, Step Functions
  • Decide when to use containers and when to use serverless
  • Choose load balancers, caches, read replicas and API Gateway

2Coupling, state, scaling, load balancing and caching

Running case

Lantern and Loom Meets the Holiday Rush

  • A holiday sale multiplies traffic tenfold
  • Checkout waits for the email service, so one slow call stalls the page
  • Sessions vanish when a web server is replaced
  • Partners want order events pushed to them
  • Your job: make each part scale and fail on its own

Tight and Loose Coupling

Tightly coupled Loosely coupled
Calls Components call each other directly and wait Components talk through an intermediary
Failure One slow or failed part stalls the rest Each part fails and recovers on its own
Scaling Everything scales together Each part scales independently
  • Intermediaries: queues (SQS), topics (SNS), event buses (EventBridge), load balancers, APIs, workflows (Step Functions)
  • They absorb spikes, retry, and let you deploy separately
Exam tip

Spikes, retries or independent scaling: put a queue, topic or event bus between the components.

Stateless and Stateful Workloads

  • Stateless: the server keeps no session data between requests, so any instance can serve any request
  • Stateful: state lives on the instance, so requests must return to the same server, and a failure loses it
  • Move state out: sessions to ElastiCache or DynamoDB, files to S3 or EFS, data to databases
  • Sticky sessions pin a client to a target: a workaround, not the best design
  • Lambda is built for short tasks that keep no state between invocations
Exam tip

To scale out or replace servers freely, make the tier stateless and store state elsewhere.

Scaling Up and Scaling Out

Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out)
How A bigger instance More instances
Limits A ceiling, often a restart, one point of failure Needs a stateless design and a load balancer
Resilience Low High: lose one, keep serving
  • Web and app tiers: Auto Scaling behind a load balancer; containers scale tasks
  • Queue workers: scale on queue depth
  • Data tier: read replicas, caches, DynamoDB capacity
Exam tip

Resilient and elastic usually means scale out, which means stateless.

Multi-Tier Architectures

  • Web, application and data tiers, each in private subnets except the load balancer
  • A load balancer sits in front of each tier that needs one
  • Each tier scales on its own, across two or more AZs
  • A cache shields the database; a queue buffers background work

Exam tip

Separate the tiers so each can scale, fail and be replaced independently.

Choosing a Load Balancer

Type Layer Best for
Application (ALB) 7: HTTP and HTTPS Web apps, microservices, containers; path and host routing; Lambda targets
Network (NLB) 4: TCP, UDP, TLS Millions of requests per second, low latency, a static IP per AZ
Gateway (GWLB) 3: gateway Third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls
Classic (CLB) Previous generation Legacy; migrate to a current type
  • All spread traffic across AZs, run health checks, and scale automatically
Exam tip

HTTP routing: ALB. Static IPs or extreme performance on TCP or UDP: NLB. Appliances: GWLB.

Application Load Balancer Routing

  • A listener checks rules in priority order; each has conditions and actions
  • Route by path, host, header, method, query string or source IP
  • A target group holds instances, IP addresses or Lambda functions, with its own health checks
  • Also redirects, fixed responses, user authentication, AWS WAF and ACM certificates

Exam tip

Many services behind one URL, routed by path or host: one ALB with several target groups.

Caching Strategies

Layer Service What it caches
Edge CloudFront, a CDN Content near users (module 9)
API API Gateway cache Responses of an API stage
Application ElastiCache Query results, sessions
Database DAX DynamoDB reads
  • Lazy loading: load on a miss; caches only what is read; data can go stale
  • Write-through: update the cache on every write; never stale; extra write cost
  • Add a TTL to limit stale data and wasted space
Exam tip

Fresh data on every read: write-through. Cache only what is read: lazy loading. Use a TTL with either.

Read Replicas and Data-Tier Scaling

  • An RDS read replica is a read-only copy fed by asynchronous replication; it offloads reads
  • Replicas can be in another Region, and can be promoted to a standalone database for disaster recovery
  • Replica data can lag, so reads may be slightly stale
  • RDS does not autoscale replicas: you add them
  • A Multi-AZ standby is synchronous and cannot serve reads: it is for availability
  • Pair replicas with a cache for read-heavy workloads
Exam tip

Scale reads: read replicas or a cache. Survive a failure: Multi-AZ.

3Messaging, workflows, serverless, containers and APIs

Amazon SQS Queues [Verify live]

  • A hosted queue that decouples producers from consumers and buffers spikes
  • Standard queues: at-least-once delivery, so consumers must handle duplicates
  • FIFO queues: exactly-once processing and ordering, with a high-throughput mode
  • Visibility timeout hides a message while it is processed; the consumer deletes it when done
  • A dead-letter queue collects messages that keep failing; retention is 60 seconds to 14 days
  • As of 5 November 2026: a message holds up to 1 MiB; older material says 256 KiB
Exam tip

Buffer work and scale consumers on queue depth: SQS. Strict order: FIFO.

Amazon SNS Publish and Subscribe

  • A publisher sends to a topic; SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber
  • Subscribers: SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP(S) endpoints, email, SMS, mobile push, Firehose
  • Supports application-to-application and application-to-person messages
  • Message filtering sends each subscriber only what it needs
  • Standard and FIFO topics
  • SNS does not store messages for offline subscribers: pair it with SQS
Exam tip

One message to many consumers: SNS. Add SQS queues for durability.

Fan-Out with SNS and SQS

  • The order service publishes once to an SNS topic
  • Each queue gets a copy and is processed at its own pace
  • A slow or failed consumer does not affect the others
  • Add a subscriber without changing the publisher

Exam tip

Fan-out with SNS plus SQS: one event, many independent, durable consumers.

Amazon EventBridge [Verify live]

  • A serverless event bus that connects AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners
  • Rules match event patterns and send events to targets, with optional transformation
  • Pipes: point-to-point from one source to one target, with filtering and enrichment
  • Scheduler: cron, rate and one-time schedules
  • Built for event-driven architectures: producers do not know the consumers
  • As of 5 November 2026: the docs describe a newer Custom Event Bus and the Classic one; check which applies
Exam tip

Route events by content from many sources, or run schedules: EventBridge.

Amazon MQ

  • A managed message broker for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ
  • Supports JMS, AMQP, MQTT, OpenWire and STOMP
  • Migrate an existing broker without rewriting the messaging code
  • Messages are encrypted at rest and in transit; AWS handles setup, maintenance and upgrades
  • Multi-AZ designs keep brokers available
  • For new cloud-native apps, SQS and SNS are simpler and scale further
Exam tip

An existing application that speaks JMS or AMQP: Amazon MQ.

Choosing a Messaging Service

Need Service
Buffer work, retry, absorb spikes SQS
Strict order, exactly-once processing SQS FIFO
Push one message to many subscribers, including email and SMS SNS
Durable copies for each consumer SNS plus SQS
Route events from services and SaaS, schedules EventBridge
Migrate a JMS or AMQP broker Amazon MQ
Exam tip

Match the verb: buffer, push, route or migrate.

AWS Step Functions Workflows

Standard Express
Runs for Up to one year Up to five minutes
Execution Exactly once At least once
Start rate Hundreds of starts per second Thousands of starts per second
Use for Long-running, auditable workflows High-volume streaming and IoT
  • State machines with Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait states
  • Retry and Catch handle errors; callbacks wait for a human
  • Calls over two hundred services directly
Exam tip

Multi-step logic with retries and branches: Step Functions, not code inside a Lambda function.

AWS Lambda and Serverless Patterns [Verify live]

  • Run code without servers: Lambda scales automatically and you pay for use
  • Events from S3, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, API Gateway and DynamoDB start functions
  • Limits: 15 minutes per invocation; 128 MB to 10,240 MB of memory, with CPU in proportion; 6 MB request and response when synchronous
  • 1,000 concurrent executions per Region by default; new accounts start lower
  • Stateless: keep data in S3, DynamoDB or a database
  • As of 5 November 2026: the docs also list newer options such as Lambda Managed Instances and durable functions
Exam tip

Short, event-driven, spiky work: Lambda. Over 15 minutes: another compute option.

Containers: ECS, EKS and Fargate [Verify live]

Service What it is Choose it when
Amazon ECS AWS-native container orchestration: tasks and services You want the simplest AWS-native option
Amazon EKS Managed Kubernetes, Kubernetes-conformant You need Kubernetes compatibility or portability
AWS Fargate Serverless compute for ECS and EKS: no servers to manage You do not want to manage nodes
  • Move to containers: package the app and its dependencies in an image, store it in ECR, run it on ECS or EKS
  • On your own servers: ECS Anywhere, EKS Anywhere and EKS Distro, the open-source Kubernetes build
  • As of 5 November 2026: ECS also lists Managed Instances; EKS has Auto Mode
Exam tip

Containers without managing servers: Fargate. Kubernetes required: EKS.

Amazon API Gateway

  • A front door for REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, in front of Lambda, EC2 or any HTTP backend
  • Handles traffic management, throttling, authorization and monitoring
  • Authorizers: IAM, Lambda authorizers and Cognito user pools
  • REST APIs add caching, usage plans and API keys; HTTP APIs are simpler and cheaper
  • Canary releases, custom domains, AWS WAF and X-Ray support
  • Edge-optimized, Regional or private endpoints
Exam tip

A managed API with throttling, keys and a Lambda backend: API Gateway.

Purpose-Built Managed Services

Service Use it for
Elastic Beanstalk Upload code; it provisions instances, load balancing, scaling and monitoring; no extra charge
AWS Amplify Build and host full-stack web and mobile apps with Git-based deployment
AWS Device Farm Test web and mobile apps on real devices
Serverless Application Repository Find, deploy and publish serverless apps from SAM templates
AWS Transfer Family Managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP into S3 or EFS (module 11)
AWS Secrets Manager Store and rotate secrets such as database passwords (module 2)
Exam tip

Least operational overhead usually means a purpose-built managed service.

4Patterns, design check and practice

An Event-Driven Microservice Pattern

  • API Gateway receives the request; a function accepts the order and publishes an event
  • Queues buffer the work for payment, inventory and email workers
  • Dead-letter queues catch failures; retries are safe if workers are idempotent
  • Each microservice owns its data and scales alone

Exam tip

Accept fast, process later: acknowledge the request, then work through queues.

Lambda, Fargate or EC2?

Lambda Fargate EC2
Unit A function A container A virtual server
Run time Up to 15 minutes No fixed limit No fixed limit
You manage Code only The container The OS and scaling
Best for Event-driven, spiky, short Long-running services, batch jobs Full control, special hardware, licenses
Exam tip

Longer than 15 minutes or already a container: Fargate. Least management for short events: Lambda.

What the Exam Asks: Scalable and Loosely Coupled

  • Which coupling service: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, MQ or Step Functions
  • Which scaling approach: vertical or horizontal, stateless or stateful
  • Which load balancer or cache: ALB, NLB, GWLB, ElastiCache or a replica
  • Which compute: Lambda, Fargate, ECS, EKS or EC2
  • Which managed service: API Gateway, Beanstalk, Amplify or Transfer Family
Exam tip

Underline the requirement: least overhead, buffering, fan-out, order or portability.

Design Check: Lantern and Loom Meets the Holiday Rush

Requirement Design
Checkout waits on the email service An SQS queue and a worker
Sessions vanish when a server is replaced Stateless web tier, sessions in ElastiCache
/api and /images served by different services One ALB, path rules, two target groups
Partners need fixed IP addresses on TCP A Network Load Balancer with Elastic IPs
Catalog reads overload the database Read replicas and a cache
One order must reach three consumers SNS topic fanning out to SQS queues
Multi-step order flow with retries Step Functions
A public API with throttling and keys API Gateway
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1At Lantern and Loom, the checkout service calls the email service directly, and a slow email service delays every order. Which change makes the two components loosely coupled?

  • AGive the email service a larger instance type so it responds faster
  • BSend each email request to an SQS queue that a worker reads
  • CPut both services on the same instance to cut network latency
  • DIncrease the timeout of the direct call so checkout waits longer
Show the answer

Answer: B. A queue between the components lets checkout finish immediately while the worker sends emails at its own pace, and it buffers spikes. A bigger instance, one shared server or a longer timeout keep the components tightly coupled.

S2Lantern and Loom's web servers keep shopping-cart sessions in memory, so replacing a server logs customers out. The team wants to scale out freely. What should the architect do?

  • AEnable sticky sessions on the load balancer and keep the current design
  • BMove to a single larger instance and stop scaling out the web tier
  • CStore the sessions on the local disk of each instance in the fleet
  • DStore sessions in ElastiCache so any instance can serve any request
Show the answer

Answer: D. Moving state out of the instances makes the web tier stateless, so servers can be added or replaced without losing sessions. Sticky sessions and local disks still tie a customer to one server, and a single larger instance cannot scale out.

S3A partner needs to connect to Lantern and Loom over TCP from fixed IP addresses, with very high throughput and low latency. Which load balancer fits?

  • AA Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address per zone
  • BAn Application Load Balancer with path-based routing rules and a WAF
  • CA Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions enabled
  • DA Gateway Load Balancer in front of a firewall appliance
Show the answer

Answer: A. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4, handles very high throughput with low latency, and supports a static address per Availability Zone, including Elastic IPs. An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, Classic is the previous generation, and a Gateway Load Balancer fronts appliances.

S4The product catalog of Lantern and Loom runs on Amazon RDS and its read traffic is overloading the primary instance. Which TWO actions reduce the read load? (Select TWO.)

  • AAdd one or more RDS read replicas and send reads to them
  • BUse the Multi-AZ standby instance for read queries
  • CReduce the retention period of automated backups
  • DPlace an Amazon ElastiCache cache in front of the database
  • ETurn off synchronous replication to the standby
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Read replicas serve read-only copies of the data, and a cache answers repeated reads without reaching the database. A Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads, and changing backups or standby replication does not reduce read load.

S5Lantern and Loom wants a managed, public REST API for its mobile app, with throttling, API keys per partner and a Lambda function behind it. Which service should the architect choose?

  • AAn Application Load Balancer with a fixed response
  • BAmazon CloudFront with a Lambda origin only
  • CAmazon API Gateway REST API with usage plans and API keys
  • DAn Amazon SNS topic with an HTTP subscription
Show the answer

Answer: C. API Gateway REST APIs provide throttling, usage plans and API keys, and integrate directly with Lambda. A load balancer, a CDN or a topic do not manage per-partner keys and quotas.

S6Which TWO statements about Amazon SQS queue types are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • AStandard queues guarantee strict first-in, first-out ordering
  • BStandard queues deliver each message at least once, so consumers should tolerate duplicates
  • CFIFO queues deliver every message to many subscribers at once
  • DStandard queues automatically delete a message when it is received
  • EFIFO queues provide ordering and exactly-once processing
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Standard queues use at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, while FIFO queues add ordering and exactly-once processing. Publishing one message to many subscribers is SNS, and a consumer must delete a message after processing it.

S7When an order is placed, Lantern and Loom must notify the inventory, email and analytics systems. Each system must process messages at its own pace, and a new system must be addable without changing the order service. Which design fits?

  • AThe order service calls the inventory, email and analytics systems in turn
  • BPublish to an SNS topic that has one SQS queue per system
  • COne shared SQS queue that all three systems read from
  • DA scheduled Lambda function that polls the order database for changes
Show the answer

Answer: B. SNS fan-out copies each message to every subscribed queue, so each system has its own durable buffer and pace, and new subscribers need no change to the publisher. A single shared queue gives each message to only one consumer.

S8Lantern and Loom's refund process has several steps, needs retries, branches on the order value, and must wait for a human approval that can take days. Which service should orchestrate it?

  • AA single Lambda function that sleeps until approval
  • BAn Amazon SQS queue with a long visibility timeout
  • CAn Amazon SNS topic with email subscribers
  • DStep Functions Standard workflow with a callback
Show the answer

Answer: D. Step Functions Standard workflows run for up to a year, handle retries and choices, and can wait for a callback from a human. A Lambda function is limited to 15 minutes, and queues and topics do not orchestrate steps.

S9A nightly job at Lantern and Loom processes catalog images for about forty minutes inside a custom container. The team wants no servers to manage. Which option fits best?

  • AAn AWS Fargate task that runs the container without servers
  • BAn AWS Lambda function with the maximum timeout
  • CAn API Gateway endpoint that runs the job
  • DAn Application Load Balancer with a fixed response
Show the answer

Answer: A. Fargate runs containers without servers and has no fixed time limit. A Lambda invocation stops after 15 minutes, and an API endpoint or a load balancer does not run batch work.

S10A company is moving an on-premises application that uses JMS to talk to its message broker. It wants to keep the messaging code unchanged. Which service should it choose?

  • AAmazon SNS with an HTTP endpoint
  • BAmazon EventBridge with a custom bus
  • CAmazon MQ
  • DAmazon SQS with a long polling client
Show the answer

Answer: C. Amazon MQ is a managed broker for ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ that supports JMS and other standard protocols, so existing messaging code can move without a rewrite. SQS, SNS and EventBridge use their own APIs.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Loose coupling queues, topics, event buses and workflows between components
Scaling scale out, keep tiers stateless, cache and use read replicas
Entry points ALB for HTTP routing, NLB for static IPs and TCP or UDP, API Gateway for APIs
Messaging SQS buffers, SNS fans out, EventBridge routes, MQ migrates, Step Functions orchestrates
Compute Lambda for short events, Fargate for containers, managed services for least overhead
